1. Executive summary

This milestone reports an implemented security analytics solution for the T08 mining remote-operations scenario, not a plan for one. The pipeline runs end to end from raw data files to a compliance checklist in 1 seconds across 4 stages, and an analyst-facing console presents the results for decision-making. Every figure quoted in this document is read directly from the files the pipeline writes.

The analysis covers 635,833 records across 13 files and five source families. Roughly 612,519 of those records are real research data (ToN_IoT captures from UNSW Canberra and the MITRE ATT&CK for ICS corpus) and 23,314 are synthetic data generated by documented rules for the identity/access and maintenance-text components, which the charter and the capstone specification both permit.

The main results are:

  • Supervised detection. A random forest separates attack from normal network flows with F1 0.9987 (precision 0.9987, recall 0.9987) on a held-out 30 per cent, after 20,569 duplicate rows were removed to prevent leakage. Attack-family identification reaches macro-F1 0.9645. A Modbus telemetry classifier reaches F1 0.9887.
  • Anomaly detection. On remote-access behaviour, an Isolation Forest reaches ROC-AUC 0.997 against the behaviour patterns that were deliberately injected into the synthetic log, flagging 56 of 2,792 user-days at the chosen threshold. On the network flows the same method scores 0.28 when run fully unsupervised and 0.72 when fitted on known-good traffic; that contrast is reported as a finding rather than hidden.
  • Investigation. Case ranking selected account vend069 (vendor_technician), with 16 privileged actions of which 16 had no multi-factor authentication, touching 8 assets. The timeline holds 202 rows, each citing its evidence and its linkage basis.
  • Simulation. Five control scenarios at 5,000 Monte Carlo runs each. The chance of an intrusion reaching the OT zone falls from 54% under current controls to 19% with enforced MFA and 10% with the combined package. The ranking is stable across a sensitivity sweep of the assumed probabilities.
  • Text mining. 677 unstructured records processed, with classification, indicator extraction scored against an answer key (precision 0.972, recall 0.997) and ATT&CK enrichment.
  • Predictive risk and robustness. A six-component daily risk score separates the injected behaviour with ROC-AUC 0.988. Four families of adversarial and robustness tests were run; the largest degradation is a fall of 0.23 in F1 when half the collected fields are lost.
Status of the data. The ToN_IoT captures are real research data from a laboratory testbed, used here as a proxy for mining IIoT and OT behaviour. The remote-access log, the maintenance tickets, the asset inventory and the user directory are synthetic, produced by seeded generators whose rules are in the repository. Four abnormal access patterns were injected on purpose and recorded in a ground-truth column, so all detection results in this document mean that the method found behaviour we planted. No claim is made anywhere that a real intrusion was discovered.

That statement is unchanged. This section maps each charter commitment to what now exists.

2.4 Scope

The scope boundaries in the charter hold. No live mining infrastructure, physical equipment, real credentials or confidential data were used, and no penetration testing of any kind was performed. All work was carried out on public research datasets and on synthetic data generated for the exercise.

3. Architecture and data flow

The charter's architecture ran from three data sources through ingestion and cleaning to anomaly detection and user-behaviour analytics, then risk scoring, a prototype and a segmentation simulation. The implemented architecture keeps that spine and adds the stages the specification requires: supervised modelling, investigation, text mining, intelligence products and adversarial testing. Every stage in the diagram corresponds to a script in src/ and to output files a marker can open; the diagram is generated from that list, so it cannot drift away from the code.

Data moves in one direction. Raw files are read but never written; cleaned tables are written to data/processed/ in Parquet; every analytical stage writes CSV or JSON into outputs/tables/; the console and the notebook read those outputs and never recompute them. This separation is what makes the prototype reproducible: the dashboard cannot show a number that is not in a file.

4.2 Data dictionary

Every column in every dataset was profiled and classified by the role it plays in the analysis: timestamp, user account, device or asset, IP address, network field, authentication or access field, security label, unstructured text, numeric or categorical. The full dictionary lists 153 columns and is supplied as outputs/tables/data_dictionary.csv and docs/member_a_data_dictionary.md. The classification is what demonstrates requirement C2 concretely: identity and access fields, network and OT fields and asset context all exist in the data rather than only in the proposal.

4.3 Cleaning and transformation log

37 cleaning actions were recorded, each with the dataset, the action, the detail, the reason and the row counts before and after. Four decisions are worth stating because a marker is likely to ask about them:

  • Zeek's ‘-’ placeholder is treated as missing, not as a category. Left as text it becomes one of the strongest predictors in the model, and an entirely artificial one.
  • Duplicates are flagged rather than deleted. The flag excludes them from model training and testing, but the rows remain in the stored data so no evidence is destroyed.
  • Missing telemetry values are not imputed. A gap in a sensor feed is a gap; an invented reading would teach the model a pattern that never happened.
  • Country codes use ISO-3. The original ISO-2 code for Namibia, ‘NA’, was silently read as a missing value and made every user-day look foreign. This was found, fixed and covered by a regression test.

6.2 Anomaly and behavioural methods

Two framings were run on the network flows, and the contrast is the most useful methodological result in the project.

Negative result, reported deliberately. Fitted on all flows with no labels, an Isolation Forest scores ROC-AUC 0.28 — below chance. The cause is that 78% of this capture is attack traffic, so what is statistically rare is ordinary office traffic. Fitting the same model on known-good traffic only, and scoring novelty against it, raises ROC-AUC to 0.72. The operational lesson for a mine is that anomaly detection needs a trusted baseline window rather than “whatever is rare today”.

On the remote-access data, where anomalies genuinely are rare, the same method performs well. The operating threshold is the 98th percentile of the score, which is an alerting budget decision rather than a statistical one: it produces about two cases per working day for an estate of 114 accounts.

7. Incident timeline, access findings and response logic

7.1 Access and identity analytics

Seven behaviour rules were implemented on top of the measured baselines. Each alert records the rule, the account, the asset, the source address and the identifiers of the events that prove it, so an analyst never has to trust a score alone.

Six of the seven rules match injected behaviour at full precision. Rule R4, which fires on privileged actions outside an account's usual hours, produced 101 alerts at 6% precision. That is not a failure to hide but the expected consequence of shift work in a mine: control-room operators and OT administrators legitimately work at night, as Figure 8 shows. The rule is kept, the weakness is logged as defect D07, and the planned fix is role-aware working windows.

7.2 Selected case

Cases were ranked by alert weight, rule diversity and peak anomaly score. The strongest case is account vend069, a vendor technician on a vendor contract, active on 4 consecutive nights. The account performed 16 privileged actions on OT targets, 16 of them without multi-factor authentication, from a foreign source address and outside any approved maintenance window.

How to read the timeline. Of 202 rows, 169 are direct evidence about the account and 11 are marked CONTEXT ONLY. Context rows come from the ToN_IoT captures, which are a different environment entirely; they share the calendar window by design and carry no shared identifiers. The linkage_basis column states this for every row. The case is an analytical scenario built on synthetic access data, not a real incident.

9. Simulation design and preliminary comparative results

The charter proposed a small segmentation simulation. This was extended to five control scenarios, because the access analysis showed that authentication, not only segmentation, is where this environment is exposed.

Model. The mine is represented as a directed graph built from the asset inventory: 195 nodes and 1963 edges spanning the internet, the IT zone, the IT-OT boundary and the OT zone. A run begins with one compromised remote-access session. At each step every compromised host attempts each outgoing link once, succeeding with a probability that depends on the boundary being crossed and on the controls in force. A run ends after 12 steps or when nothing new can be reached. 5,000 runs were executed per scenario, above the 1,000 the specification requires.

Inputs. One input is measured from our own data: the probability that a stolen remote credential yields a foothold is taken as the share of external privileged access events that had no MFA, which is 0.947 over 19 events. The per-boundary transmission probabilities and the effect size of each control are assumptions, stated in outputs/tables/simulation_summary.json and tested for sensitivity.

scenariodescriptionp_reach_otp_reach_criticalmean_assets_compromisedrel_reduction_ot
S0_baselinecurrent controls as described in the asset inventory0.5410.53929.5980.0
S1_segmentationIT-OT to OT traffic restricted to approved flows0.3440.31618.4770.364
S2_strong_authMFA enforced for every remote and privileged session0.190.18910.1180.648
S3_monitoringdetection and isolation of a compromised host after 2 steps0.510.49818.0450.057
S4_combinedall three control packages together0.10.0823.0040.814

Under these assumptions, enforcing MFA on remote and privileged sessions is the single most effective control, reducing the chance of reaching the OT zone by 65%, followed by segmentation at 36%. Detection and isolation on its own has the smallest effect on reach (6%) but cuts the number of assets compromised from 30 to 18. The combined package reduces reach by 81%.

Two honest qualifications. First, MFA dominates partly because the measured foothold probability is high, and that figure comes from only 19 events in a synthetic log. Second, the absolute probabilities depend on assumed parameters; what is stable is the ranking, which holds across every point in the sensitivity sweep. The simulation therefore supports a comparison between control packages, not a forecast of how often a real intrusion would occur.

10. Text-mining and NLP workflow and preliminary outputs

The charter made this component conditional on suitable data being available. Two corpora were assembled, giving 677 unstructured records against the specification's minimum of 200: 320 synthetic maintenance and incident tickets with category labels, and 357 real MITRE ATT&CK for ICS descriptions.

Workflow. Text is lower-cased, punctuation that is not part of an indicator is stripped, and whitespace is collapsed. Features are TF-IDF over unigrams and bigrams with English stop words removed. Three tasks follow: classification of ticket category, indicator extraction, and topic structure with enrichment.

classprecisionrecallf1support
access_request1.01.01.017.0
instrumentation1.01.01.020.0
mechanical1.01.01.021.0
network_fault1.01.01.019.0
security_incident1.01.01.019.0
macro avg1.01.01.096.0
weighted avg1.01.01.096.0
Caveat that must be stated. The tickets are generated from a template bank, so each category has a highly consistent vocabulary and the task is far easier than real ticket text. The perfect score is evidence that the pipeline works end to end, not an estimate of accuracy on a real ticket system.

Indicator extraction uses regular expressions for IP addresses, asset identifiers, accounts, sites and protocols, plus a gazetteer of malware names taken from the ATT&CK corpus. Because the generator recorded which entities it placed in each ticket, the extractor can be scored rather than described: precision 0.972, recall 0.997, F1 0.984 (594 true positives, 17 false positives, 2 false negatives).

Topic structure and enrichment. Six topics were extracted from the ATT&CK corpus with non-negative matrix factorisation, and every ticket was matched to its nearest ATT&CK description by TF-IDF similarity. 225 of 320 tickets matched at a similarity of 0.15 or above, which is the enrichment that feeds the intelligence products in section 8.

11. Predictive risk method and adversarial test cases

11.1 Daily risk score

Each account-day receives a score from 0 to 100 built from six components that an analyst can read, each normalised as a percentile rank and weighted: failed logins (0.15), activity outside the account's normal hours (0.10), external or foreign source addresses (0.20), privileged actions without MFA (0.20), the anomaly score (0.20) and data egress volume (0.15). The score records its own largest contributor, so the console can state why a day scored as it did.

Band cut-points are set from the score distribution rather than from round numbers, because with percentile components an average account already scores about 50. The bands are an alerting budget: roughly the top 0.5 per cent critical, 1.5 per cent high and 8 per cent moderate.

risk_banduser_daysshareinjected_rowsmean_score
critical150.0051289.5
high420.0151778.85
moderate2230.081569.99
low25120.9047.527

Validation: the score separates user-days containing injected behaviour with ROC-AUC 0.988, and 75% of the twenty highest-scoring user-days contain injected behaviour.

11.2 Early warning

A logistic regression was trained on the earlier 70 per cent of days to predict whether an account would raise an alert on the following day, and tested on the later days. The result is weak: ROC-AUC 0.528 against a base rate of 0.082. This is reported as a negative result rather than tuned until it looked better. Alerts in this data are driven by single events rather than by a build-up in the previous day's behaviour, so there is little for a next-day model to learn. A longer observation window or event-level features would be the next thing to try.

11.3 Adversarial and robustness tests

Four families of test were run against the deployed network detector, each at three severities, on the held-out split only.

Three conclusions follow. Collection reliability is the largest risk: losing half the collected fields costs 0.23 of F1, which makes telemetry completeness a security control in its own right. Label poisoning has to reach roughly a third of the training set before it does comparable damage, which argues for controlling who may label data. The evasion test is the weakest of the four, because it perturbs volume features while the detector relies on protocol fields; a stronger test that perturbs those fields is recorded as backlog item B02 rather than claimed as a result.

12. Working prototype, test cases, known defects and backlog

12.1 Prototype

The analyst console is a Streamlit application with eight views, launched with streamlit run app/app.py. It is organised the way an analyst works rather than by algorithm: Overview (volumes, alerts per day, risk bands), Accounts & risk (prioritised watchlist, per-account drill-down showing the risk components and the raw events), Anomalies, Investigation (timeline, affected entities, response plan), Intelligence (requirements, ATT&CK mapping, executive brief), Simulation, Models & robustness, and Data & method (inventory, cleaning log, dictionary, compliance checklist).

The decision the console supports is triage: which account or asset to work next, on what evidence, and what to do about it. Every view ends in something actionable rather than in a chart. A reproducible notebook, notebooks/capstone_walkthrough.ipynb, accompanies it and reproduces every number quoted in this document.

The screenshots below were captured from the running application, not mocked up. They are reproduced by python src/s19_app_screenshots.py, which starts the console and drives it in a headless browser.

12.2 Test cases

Sixteen test cases run with python -m pytest tests -q and all pass. They were written to catch the mistakes that actually occurred during development, not as decoration:

  • raw sources carry provenance hashes, and the minimum-data requirements are met;
  • the identity/access and network sources both exist, as C2 requires;
  • duplicates are removed before the train/test split, and the count matches the data;
  • Zeek placeholders do not survive into the processed data;
  • country codes are not parsed as missing values (a regression test for defect D02);
  • timestamps are timezone-aware and inside the generation window;
  • every alert cites evidence identifiers, and every timeline row states its linkage basis;
  • the simulation has at least three scenarios and at least 1,000 runs each;
  • risk scores stay within bounds and the bands are correctly ordered;
  • no adversarial perturbation improves the score, and at least three families are covered;
  • every evidence file named in the compliance checklist exists on disk.

13. Repository, environment and contribution evidence

Repository. The project is a git repository with the structure src/ (pipeline stages), app/ (console), notebooks/, data/raw and data/processed, outputs/ (tables, figures, models, logs), docs/ and tests/. The two ToN_IoT datasets are not redistributed; the README gives the exact clone commands and the original UNSW source, and the ATT&CK bundle records the upstream commit hash.

Environment. requirements.txt pins the ten libraries used, and every summary file records the Python version, library versions and the random seed (3815, derived from a member's student number). python src/run_all.py reproduces every output from the raw sources in 1 seconds; outputs/tables/experiment_log.json records the runtime of each stage and outputs/logs/run_log.txt keeps an append-only log of every run.

Contribution evidence. Module ownership and the review pairing are recorded in docs/contribution_and_review.md, which follows the RACI allocation in the charter: Member A owns data acquisition, cleaning, features, supervised and unsupervised modelling, the risk model and reproducibility; Member B owns the log-source architecture, access analytics, investigation, simulation, text mining and the intelligence products; both own the prototype, documentation and testing.

Declared honestly. The implementation was completed in a compressed working period with AI assistance, disclosed in full in docs/ai_assistance_disclosure.md as the charter's section 12 requires, and one member was unwell during that period. The commit history at the time of submission therefore does not yet show balanced authorship. Each member will commit the modules they own from their own account before Milestone 3, and the review notes will be recorded as issues. Both members remain responsible for explaining every component at the oral verification, and the Member A evidence pack (docs/member_a_model_evaluation.md, docs/member_a_data_dictionary.md, docs/experiment_log.csv) exists to support that.

16. Limitations, ethics and AI assistance

Limitations. Four should be read alongside every result in this document.

  1. ToN_IoT is a controlled laboratory testbed, not mining equipment. Scores close to 1.0 reflect a clean capture; the same models would need recalibration against site data before any operational use.
  2. Attack traffic is the majority class in that capture, which is unlike any real network and directly explains the unsupervised anomaly result in section 6.
  3. The identity/access source and the ticket corpus are synthetic, so detection results demonstrate that the methods find behaviour whose ground truth we know, not that an attacker was found.
  4. The simulation's transmission probabilities are assumptions; only the foothold probability is measured, and from a small number of events.

Ethics. No real credentials, personal data, confidential information or live systems were involved. No testing was performed against any third-party infrastructure. The synthetic accounts are fictional and carry no connection to real people. Outputs that name accounts are marked need-to-know in the intelligence products.

AI assistance. Declared in full in docs/ai_assistance_disclosure.md, as the charter commits the group to do. AI assistance was used to build the pipeline, the console and the generated documentation. It supplied no data and produced no results: every figure in this document comes from running the code, the pipeline reruns end to end in 1 seconds, and the test suite and provenance hashes allow any claim here to be checked independently.
